state.case_summary:
A woman in her 60s with a history of hypertension presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset chest pain. She had no history of any acute febrile illness or family history of sudden cardiac death.

Patient was tachycardic with a pulse of 120 beats/min. Her blood pressure was normal.

- Laboratory tests:    - White blood cell count: 14,300/µL (normal range: 3500-9500/µL)    - Serum calcium: within normal limits    - High-sensitivity troponin I: 1.15 ng/mL (normal range: <0.015 ng/mL)    - Brain-type natriuretic peptide: 1060.30 pg/mL (normal range: 0-100 pg/mL)  - ECG findings:    Image Title: Electrocardiograms at Admission and Different Time Points    Image Description: Initial ECG showed sinus tachycardia, PR-segment elevation in lead aVR, PR-segment depression in leads I, II, III, aVF, and V4 to V6. ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF, and V2 to V6, with ST-segment depression in lead aVR.  - Imaging studies:    - Coronary angiography: revealed normal coronary arteries    - Left ventriculography: confirmed systolic apical ballooning    - Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT: revealed an enhanced left-adrenal heterogeneous mass measuring 4.1 × 3.4 cm

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Pheochromocytoma-induced cardiomyopathy
B. Primary Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy
C. Pheochromocytoma crisis
D. Acute pericarditis

Pulmonary embolism: no mention of respiratory symptoms or findings

systolic apical ballooning on left ventriculography
